61: 
62: ## 1. Design principles (DSL-flavored)
63: 
64: These recap the protocol's non-negotiables in author-facing terms. A conformant
65: DSL must be *shaped* by them:
66: 
67: - **Declarative structure, never positions.** The DSL expresses `WHAT` — a
68:   `VStack`, a `HStack`, a `Text` — and constraint properties (spacing, padding,
69:   alignment, size hints). It never computes bounds and never emits rects.
70: - **Exactly three authoring operations.** Every view exposes the same three
71:   operations — **configure values** (§5.0 `with`), **apply modifiers**
72:   (`modifiers`), and, for content-bearing views, **supply children**
73:   (`children`). The three are a single fluent builder: any of them may be the
74:   first call and they may be chained in **any order** (see
75:   [§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)); a later call overrides an earlier
76:   value for the same property.
77: - **`body()` is evaluated once at mount.** A composite view declares its
78:   subtree once; reactivity comes from **signals**, never from re-evaluating the
79:   body. This is what lets the emitter produce fine-grained
80:   `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE` deltas instead of rebuilding the tree.
81:   The one sanctioned exception is a **structural container**
82:   ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)): its content is
83:   re-evaluated on a signal change and the emitter reconciles the retained
84:   subtree into `TREE` deltas.
85: - **Modifiers are decoupled from views — and never hard-bound to a view
86:   type.** Any modifier applies to any view (`.padding` works on a `Text` and a
87:   `VStack` alike), and any developer can **author a custom modifier in
88:   application code** (a `ViewModifier`) that applies to any existing view —
89:   library primitive, container, control, custom view, or an already-modified
90:   view (see [§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)). A modifier a
91:   given renderer cannot apply is **allowed and ignored** — the property is
92:   still emitted.
93: - **There is exactly one modifier mechanism.** Built-in core modifiers are
94:   **not** a separate syntax: they are `ViewModifier` values the library ships,
95:   composed into a view through the shared `modifiers(...)` operation. There is
96:   **no per-modifier sugar on the view type** — `Padding` applied via
97:   `.modifiers(Padding.with(p -> p.uniform(16)))`. Core and application-authored
98:   modifiers share the same surface.
99: - **A modifier's type is named for the modifier it applies — never with a
100:   `Mod` suffix.** Where a modifier applies a single value (a font, a font
101:   weight, an alignment, a style), the value type itself MAY *be* the modifier
102:   (`FontWeight.BOLD`, `Font.headline()`, `MyButtonStyle`), so there is one name
103:   for the concept. Languages that cannot merge the two (e.g. C#, whose enums
104:   cannot implement interfaces) use the equivalent value form. See
105:   [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules).
106: - **There is exactly one style mechanism.** A customizable control/view takes
107:   its **content** from a *style* value (`ButtonStyle`, `LabelStyle`,
108:   `AudioStyle`, `VideoStyle`, …) scoped through the environment; the control
109:   owns its native component + interaction and the style owns the content
110:   ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)). Closed-variant/token
111:   styles (`ToggleStyle`, `PickerStyle`, `TextStyle`) are the same surface.
112: - **Values vs modifiers.** Structural/layout parameters and a control's bound
113:   value (`alignment`, `spacing`, `text`, `isOn`, `selection`) are **values**
114:   configured through `with(...)`. Everything decorative (padding, color, font,
115:   frame, border, …) is a **modifier** applied through `modifiers(...)`.
116: - **`Color` is never a modifier.** `Color` has SwiftUI's dual identity: it is a
117:   **View** (a layout-greedy solid-color fill) and a **Data Type** (passed into
118:   style-taking modifiers: `.foregroundStyle`, `.background`, `.border`,
119:   `.tint`). There is **no** `.color()` modifier, and `.foregroundColor(_:)` is
120:   deprecated — foreground styling is always `.foregroundStyle(_:)`.
121: - **Only changes are transmitted.** Emission is diff-based; an unchanged tree
122:   emits **zero** opcodes. The DSL describes values; the emitter diffs them.
123: - **Typed enums, never raw ints.** Every enumerated value is a typed constant
124:   (`Alignment.leading`, `FontWeight.bold`, `ToggleStyle.checkbox`), not a bare
125:   integer. The numeric code is the DSL's job to resolve (see the value-type and
126:   enum tables in MODIFIERS.md).
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 2. Canonical signature notation
131: 
132: The canonical signatures below are written SwiftUI-shaped and language
133: agnostic. Conventions used:
134: 
135: - `View(config:)` / `T("…")` — a view/control constructed with its **values**.
136: - `{ ... }` — the child subtree (a trailing closure in SwiftUI; a vararg,
137:   macro, builder, or lambda in other languages).
138: - `Signal<T>` — a read-only derived or writable signal; `WritableSignal<T>` —
139:   a two-way binding target. A control takes a `WritableSignal<T>` for its
140:   value (see [§3](#3-state-model-signals)).
141: - `()` — the action a `Button` fires.
142: - `.modifier(m)` — apply a **modifier value** to a view; chainable on any
143:   view. Every modifier — built-in or application-authored — is such a value
144:   ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)).
145: - Modifiers chain and are applied **innermost-first** (the last chained
146:   modifier's property wins).
147: 
148: ### The three operations
149: 
150: Every concrete view exposes the same three operations. They form one fluent
151: **builder**: any of the three may be the first call, and they may be chained in
152: any order. A later call overrides an earlier value for the same property.
153: 
154: | Operation | Purpose | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) |
155: |-----------|---------|----------------------------|
156: | **values** | Configure structural/layout values and a control's bound value | `View(config:)` — labels in the constructor |
157: | **modifiers** | Apply `ViewModifier` values, innermost-first | `.modifier(_:)` / `.padding(_:)` / … |
158: | **children** | Supply the content subtree (content-bearing views only) | trailing closure `{ … }` |
159: 
160: The **canonical builder spelling** (the recommended form; per-language spellings
161: are in [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)) is:
162: 
163: ```
164: ViewName.with { values }              // values   — a config-builder lambda
165:       .modifiers(modifier, ...)       // modifiers — varargs
166:       .children(view, ...)            // children  — varargs, content-bearing views only
167: ```
168: 
169: Any of the three may start the chain, e.g. all of these are equivalent:
170: 
171: ```
172: VStack.with { v in v.spacing(8) }.children(a, b).modifiers(m)
173: VStack.children(a, b).with { v in v.spacing(8) }.modifiers(m)
174: VStack.modifiers(m).children(a, b).with { v in v.spacing(8) }
175: ```
176: 
177: **Values are a config-builder lambda.** `with { c in … }` populates a per-view
178: fluent **config** (`VStack.Config`, `Text.Config`, …). It is the *same type* a
179: style's `makeBody(Config)` receives ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
180: The builder is **fluent and mutable**: setters return the config. Config-less
181: views (`Divider`, `Spacer`) take an empty `with()`.
182: 
183: **Every value member is reactive-capable (MUST).** A config member that carries a
184: value exposes **two forms** — a raw value and a `Signal<T>`:
185: 
186: ```
187: Text.with(t -> t.text("hi"))            ≡  Text.with(t -> t.text(constant("hi")))
188: Visible.with(v -> v.visible(flagSignal))      // reactive visibility
189: Frame.with(f -> f.width(widthSignal))         // reactive sizing, layout included
190: ```
191: 
192: The **raw form is sugar for a constant signal**; a **non-constant** signal
193: becomes a **node-level binding** — a change re-emits only that node's `SET_TEXT`
194: / `SET_PROPERTY`, and a constant emits as a plain property with **zero binding
195: overhead**. This holds for *every* value member, layout included
196: (`spacing`, `alignment`, `padding`, `frame`, `columns`, …): anything describable
197: in the protocol can animate. A control's two-way *value* takes a
198: `WritableSignal<T>`; every other member takes a one-way `Signal<T>`.

901: ### 5.6 Custom modifiers (developer-authored)
902: 
903: In SwiftUI any developer can define a modifier that applies to **any** existing
904: view — and Pathland is the same. This is a **first-class, MUST** property of
905: every conformant DSL: modifiers are never hard-bound to a view type.
906: 
907: - **Applicable to any view.** A modifier works on a library primitive
908:   (`Text`), a container (`VStack`), a control (`Button`), a custom view, or an
909:   already-modified view. The same modifier value applies everywhere.
910: - **One mechanism.** Core and application-authored modifiers are the **same
911:   surface**: a `ViewModifier` value applied via `.modifiers(...)`. There is
912:   **no per-modifier sugar on the view type**; a parameterized modifier is
913:   constructed with `Modifier.with(...)` and single-value modifiers pass the
914:   value directly ([§5.0](#50-authoring-a-modifier)).
915: 
916: | | Canonical | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) |
917: |-|-----------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
918: | authoring | `struct Card: ViewModifier { func body(content: Content) -> some View }` | `@FunctionalInterface ViewModifier { View body(View content) }` | `trait ViewModifier { fn apply(&mut Node) }` |
919: | applying | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifiers(Card.with(c -> …))` / `content.modifiers(A, B)` | `content.modifiers(Card)` |
920: | single-value | `.modifier(Padding(16))` | `content.modifiers(Padding.with(p -> p.uniform(16)))` | `content.modifiers(Padding(16.0))` |

The problem: The `View.with(ViewModifier...)` default method (View.java:66) still exists as a "general modifier chain", which status.md says is **removed** in favor of `.modifiers(...)`. The demo (and tests, and BorderedButtonStyle) still use `.with(Modifier...)` for modifiers:

1. `MusicPlayerView.java:110-112` — `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` on PlayerBar builder — the PlayerBar construction in MusicPlayerView
2. `MusicPlayerView.java:118` — `NowPlayingSidebar.with(...).with(Clipped.with())`
3. `MusicPlayerView.java:125-127` — `SizeThatFits.with(...).with(Frame..., AccessibilityRole...)` — SizeThatFits.with returns a `View` (FitSlot), so `.with(ViewModifier...)` is the View default
4. `ColorSection.java:40` — `accent.get().with(Frame...)` — accent is a Signal<Color>? Actually `accent.get()` returns a `Color`, and `.with(...)` on a Color applies modifiers (Color is a View). Wait Color... let me check. Actually ColorSection line 40 `accent.get().with(Frame.with(...))`. `accent` is a `State<Color>` or `Signal<Color>`? `.get()` returns `Color`. Is `Color` a View? Yes per DSL Color is a View (layout-greedy fill). So `.with(Frame...)` on a Color — uses View.with(ViewModifier).
5. `BorderedButtonStyle.java:66` — `config.label().with(ForegroundStyle..., Padding..., Background..., Border...)` — label() is a View, uses View.with(ViewModifier)
6. Tests: `RouterTest.java:626` `probe.with(BorderedButtonStyle.INSTANCE)`, `RouterTest.java:721` `root.with(EnvironmentBinding...)`, `LabelTest.java:187` `probe.with(IconOnlyLabelStyle.INSTANCE)`, `SplitNavDemoTest.java:52` `new SplitNavDemo().with(EnvironmentBinding...)`

Now, the user's complaint: "PlayerBar does not follow same principles. Uses with for Modifiers."

The key: `ViewBuilder` has `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` and `.with(Consumer<C>)`. So `PlayerBar.with(p -> p...).with(Border..., Shadow...)` — the second `.with(...)` call on the `ViewBuilder` picks up... which overload? `ViewBuilder` has `with(Consumer<C>)` and inherits `View.with(ViewModifier...)` from the interface. `Border.with` / `Shadow.with(10)` return `Border` / `Shadow` which are `ViewModifier`s, not `Consumer`. So it resolves to `View.with(ViewModifier...)` — the general modifier chain. The result type is `View` (not ViewBuilder), so it converts to a plain view.

So the fix: replace `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` with `.modifiers(Border..., Shadow...)` in PlayerBar construction (MusicPlayerView line 110). The result of `.modifiers(...)` on ViewBuilder returns a ViewBuilder, which is fine nested in children().

Now: should we also remove the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` default method entirely, to enforce the "exactly one modifier mechanism" (`modifiers(...)`)? status.md says it "are removed" — but it's clearly still present in View.java:66. That's a latent inconsistency.

Two options:
- **Option A (minimal):** Just fix the demo code (PlayerBar and siblings) to use `.modifiers(...)` instead of `.with(...)` where a builder or view gets modifiers. And in `SizeThatFits` case etc, use `.modifiers(...)`. But `View` interface has no `.modifiers(...)`. So for plain `View` values like `config.label()` and `accent.get()` and `SizeThatFits.with(...)`, `.modifiers(...)` doesn't exist. This is the crux.

- **Option B (full):** Add `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)` to the `View` interface (renaming or alongside `with(ViewModifier...)`), updating status.md claim that `with(ViewModifier...)` general chain is removed, migrate all call sites to `.modifiers(...)`. This enforces the spec: "exactly three operations — configure values (with), apply modifiers (modifiers), supply children (children)" and §5.6 says `content.modifiers(A, B)`.

Hmm, but wait. Let me re-read status.md claim precisely: "the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general modifier chain in favor of `.modifiers(...)`, and the `*Mod` shims ... are **removed**". So status claims `View.with(ViewModifier...)` was removed and replaced by `.modifiers(...)`. But `View.with(ViewModifier...)` is still in View.java:66! So either it was intended to be removed but wasn't, or status.md is ahead of the code.

Given the user is complaining about the demo not following principles, the right move per the spec and status.md is: `.modifiers(...)` should be THE one modifier mechanism, and `View.with(ViewModifier...)` should not be used in the demo. 

Actually, let me reconsider. The spec DSL.md §5.6 table: "applying | content.modifier(Card()) | content.modifiers(Card.with(c -> …)) / content.modifiers(A, B)". So the Java DSL uses `.modifiers(...)`. The spec §1: "There is exactly one modifier mechanism... composed into a view through the shared modifiers(...) operation." So the canonical operation name is `modifiers(...)`.

For `ViewBuilder` the chainable `.modifiers(...)` already exists (ViewBuilder.java:40). For plain `View` values, there's no `.modifiers(...)` — only `.with(ViewModifier...)`. So to fully align, we'd add a default `modifiers(ViewModifier...)` to `View`, and either remove or deprecate `with(ViewModifier...)`.

Actually wait — let me check: does the spec's canonical "three operations" require `.modifiers(...)` on the View interface? Looking at DSL.md §2 lines 154-167: The Java realization per §9.3... Let me check §9.3 quickly for how modifiers apply to a bare View.

Actually, the key question: is `View.with(ViewModifier...)` the intended general modifier chain? Let me look at how the demo currently builds PlayerBar. Actually the issue is in MusicPlayerView:110-112:

```
.children(PlayerBar.with(p -> p
        .trackIndex(...)...
        .volumeRequest(volumeRequest.signal()))
        .with(
                Border.with(...),
                Shadow.with(10))),
```

Here `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` calls `View.with(ViewModifier...)`. As `PlayerBar.with(...)` returns `ViewBuilder`, but `ViewBuilder` doesn't have `.with(ViewModifier...)`, only `.with(Consumer)`. Wait — it resolves via the `View` interface default `with(ViewModifier...)`. Actually since ViewBuilder implements View, `builder.with(Border, Shadow)` resolves to `View.with(ViewModifier...)`. That returns `View`. And then `.with(...)` — the arg Border and Shadow ARE ViewModifiers, so it resolves to the View default. OK.

So the fix at minimum: change `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` → `.modifiers(Border..., Shadow...)` in MusicPlayerView:110, `NowPlayingSidebar...with(Clipped.with())` → `.modifiers(Clipped.with())` at 118, and `SizeThatFits.with(...).with(Frame..., AccessibilityRole...)` → `.modifiers(...)` at 125 (types: `SizeThatFits.with(...)` returns a `View`; `.modifiers(...)` needs to exist on View).

So the "same principle" that PlayerBar violates is: modifiers must be applied via `.modifiers(...)`, not `.with(...)`. The reason the demo uses `.with(...)` is likely because... hmm, maybe `ViewBuilder` didn't have `.modifiers(...)` at the time? No, it has it. Or maybe the author didn't realize. 

Given the user specifically flagged PlayerBar, and given the spec says the modifier operation is `modifiers(...)`, the comprehensive fix:

1. Add `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)` to the `View` interface (so every View can apply modifiers via `.modifiers(...)`), and REMOVE `View.with(ViewModifier...)` (the general modifier chain) — fulfilling status.md's claim. But wait: that's a breaking change to the library surface. Is `View.with(ViewModifier...)` used anywhere that couldn't use `modifiers`? All uses we found pass ViewModifiers, so renaming to `modifiers` works.

But careful — `View.with(ViewModifier...)` returns `View`; `ViewBuilder.modifiers` returns `ViewBuilder<V,C>` (covariant, good). If we add `View.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` default returning `View`, ViewBuilder's `modifiers` covariant-overrides it. Actually Java: `ViewBuilder.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` returns `ViewBuilder<V,C>` which is a subtype of `View`. Java allows covariant return type overriding. And ViewBuilder currently doesn't have `@Override` but it'll still override the interface default. Good.

Hmm, but should View keep `with(ViewModifier...)` for backwards compat? Since demo module is the only consumer and we control everything, and status.md claims removal, we should actually remove it to enforce the principle. But is `with(ViewModifier...)` part of the spec surface? Let me check DSL.md §9.3 Java adaptation. Let me read that.

Actually, let me be pragmatic and check what the canonical principle intends. Let me read DSL.md §9.3 and the three-operations. The cleanest interpretation consistent with status.md:

- The three operations are `with` (values), `modifiers` (modifiers), `children` (children).
- `View` interface should expose all three as default instance methods so they work on any View: `with(Consumer)`? no — the value-config `with` is static per type. On the View interface, `.with(ViewModifier...)` is the odd one.

Wait, `View.with(ViewModifier...)` is an instance default method on View. It's the "general modifier chain". status.md says removed in favor of `.modifiers(...)`. So the intended design: `View` should NOT have `with(ViewModifier...)`; instead there should be a `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)`. Let me verify by checking if `ViewBuilder.modifiers` is the only `modifiers`. And whether any `View` (non-builder) in library/TESTS uses `.modifiers`. 

In the demo, plain views DO use `.modifiers(...)`:
- `Text.with("hi").modifiers(...)` — Text.with returns ViewBuilder, so `.modifiers` is ViewBuilder's.
- But `probe.with(IconOnlyLabelStyle.INSTANCE)` in LabelTest — `probe` is a raw `View` anonymous class. `.with(...)` there is `View.with(ViewModifier...)`. If we remove `with(ViewModifier...)` from View, this test breaks unless `View.modifiers` exists. So we'd change it to `probe.modifiers(...)`.
- `SplitNavDemoTest`: `new SplitNavDemo().with(EnvironmentBinding...)` → `.modifiers(...)`.
- `BorderedButtonStyle.makeBody`: `config.label().with(...)` — `config.label()` is a `View`. `.with(ViewModifier...)` → `.modifiers(...)`. label() returns View, not builder, so needs `View.modifiers` default. 
- `ColorSection`: `accent.get().with(Frame...)` — `accent` is `State<Color>`/`Signal<Color>`? `.get()` returns a `Color` — is Color a View? If Color implements View, `.with(Frame...)` → `.modifiers(Frame...)`. Let me check Color.

So the full fix:
1. `View.java`: replace `default View with(ViewModifier...)` with `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)` (same body). This restores the "one modifier mechanism = modifiers(...)" principle and matches status.md.
2. Update all call sites that used `.with(ViewModifier...)` → `.modifiers(...)`:
   - `BorderedButtonStyle.java:66`
   - `MusicPlayerView.java:110` (PlayerBar), `118` (NowPlayingSidebar), `125` (SizeThatFits)
   - `ColorSection.java:40`
   - Tests: `LabelTest.java:187`, `RouterTest.java:626`, `RouterTest.java:721`, `SplitNavDemoTest.java:52`

Wait, but hold on. Is removing `View.with(ViewModifier...)` the right call, or should we keep it and just fix the PlayerBar demo? The user said "PlayerBar does not follow same principles. Uses with for Modifiers." This is about the demo code pattern: using `with` for modifiers. The principle is "exactly three operations" and "modifiers(...) is the one modifier mechanism."

I think the minimal correct fix that aligns with status.md (which claims the chain is removed) is to:
- Add `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)` to `View` (so modifiers work on any View value), and remove `default View with(ViewModifier...)`.
- Migrate the `.with(ViewModifier)` call sites to `.modifiers(...)`.

But wait — would removing `View.with(ViewModifier...)` break `ViewBuilder`'s inherited behavior? ViewBuilder doesn't define `with(ViewModifier...)`, and after removal, `builder.with(Border, Shadow)` would no longer compile (good — forces `.modifiers`). But are there OTHER places that call `.with(...)` with a ViewModifier expecting the general chain? We found them all: BorderedButtonStyle, MusicPlayerView (3), ColorSection, and 4 test sites. Also check server-core, render-html, spring/quarkus demos — the earlier grep across main src of those dirs didn't find `.with(ViewModifier)` beyond what we have. Now I have the full picture. Let me understand the issue clearly.

The complaint: "PlayerBar does not follow same principles. Uses with for Modifiers."

Looking at `MusicPlayerView.java:103-112`:
```java
.children(PlayerBar.with(p -> p
        .trackIndex(trackIndex.signal())
        ...
        .volumeRequest(volumeRequest.signal()))
        .with(
                Border.with(b -> b.color(MusicPlayerView.BAR_BORDER).width(1).radius(500)),
                Shadow.with(10))),
```

Here `PlayerBar.with(...)` returns a `ViewBuilder<PlayerBar, Config>`. Then `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` is called. This uses the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` default method (View.java:66) — applying modifiers via `with` instead of `modifiers`. 

Also `NowPlayingSidebar.with(...).with(Clipped.with())` (MusicPlayerView.java:118), and `SizeThatFits.with(Fit...).with(Frame..., AccessibilityRole...)` (MusicPlayerView.java:125-127).

Also `accent.get().with(Frame...)` in ColorSection.java:40 — accent is a `State<Color>`... wait, `accent.get()` returns a `Color`, and `Color` implements `View`. So `.with(Frame...)` is `View.with(ViewModifier...)` on a Color. Hmm — but is that deliberate? It's applying a Frame modifier to a Color view.

And `BorderedButtonStyle.java:66`: `config.label().with(ForegroundStyle..., Padding..., Background..., Border...)` — `label()` returns a `View`, so `.with(...)` here is the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general chain.

Now, the spec/status says: "the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general modifier chain in favor of `.modifiers(...)`, and the `*Mod` shims ... are **removed**". But the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` default method still exists in View.java:66! So either:
1. The principle is that `.modifiers(...)` should be used for modifiers, and `View.with(ViewModifier...)` should be removed (per the status claim that it was removed).
2. OR the `View` interface's `with(ViewModifier...)` is a leftover that should be removed.

Given the status.md at line 41-42 explicitly states `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general modifier chain "in favor of `.modifiers(...)`" is **removed**, but it's still present in View.java:66 and still being used in the demo and library, this is a real inconsistency.

The principle established (issue #140 chain order): `.modifiers(...)` first (single call, all modifiers), then `.with(...)`, then `.children(...)`. And modifiers applied via `.modifiers(...)`.

The user says "PlayerBar does not follow same principles. Uses with for Modifiers." So the fix: in PlayerBar usage, the modifiers (Border, Shadow) should be applied via `.modifiers(...)` instead of `.with(...)`.

But wait — there's a subtlety. `PlayerBar.with(p -> p...)` returns a `ViewBuilder<PlayerBar, Config>`. `ViewBuilder` HAS a `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` method (ViewBuilder.java:40). So `.modifiers(Border..., Shadow...)` would work and return a `ViewBuilder`. But `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` — ViewBuilder only has `with(Consumer<C>)`; so `.with(Border..., Shadow...)` resolves to the inherited `View.with(ViewModifier...)` default method, returning a plain `View`. That's the inconsistency: using `with` for modifiers.

So the fix should be:
1. Change `PlayerBar.with(...).with(Border..., Shadow...)` → `.modifiers(Border..., Shadow...)` in MusicPlayerView. But per issue #140 chain order, the canonical order is `.modifiers(...)` first, then `.with(...)`. Hmm, let me think about what the canonical order should be for PlayerBar.

Actually wait — the issue #140 convention: "modifiers → with → children" order. So for PlayerBar, it should be:
```
PlayerBar.with(p -> p...
        ...
        .volumeRequest(...))
        .modifiers(
                Border.with(...),
                Shadow.with(10))
```
OR
```
PlayerBar
        .modifiers(
                Border.with(...),
                Shadow.with(10))
        .with(p -> p...)
```
The issue #140 convention is `.modifiers(...)` first. But `PlayerBar.with(p -> p...)` is the primary construction (values). Hmm. Let me check what the other demo code does.

Look at NowPlayingSidebar usage in MusicPlayerView:118: `NowPlayingSidebar.with(s -> s.trackIndex(trackIndex.signal())).with(Clipped.with())` — this applies a modifier via `.with(...)`. Should be `.modifiers(Clipped.with())`.

And MusicPlayerView:122-127: `SizeThatFits.with(Fit.of(...), Fit.of(...)).with(Frame..., AccessibilityRole...)` — SizeThatFits.with returns a `View` (FitSlot), not a ViewBuilder. So `.with(Frame..., AccessibilityRole...)` uses `View.with(ViewModifier...)`. To apply `.modifiers(...)` we'd need FitSlot to have `modifiers` — but it's a plain View. Hmm.

Wait — this is important. `.modifiers(...)` only exists on `ViewBuilder`. Plain `View` values (like `SizeThatFits.with(...)` returns, or `config.label()` returns, or `Color` values) don't have `.modifiers()`. They only have `.with(ViewModifier...)` from the `View` interface default.

So there's a real question: how does a plain `View` value apply modifiers? The DSL spec §5.6 says `content.modifiers(A, B)` — and the Java column example is `content.modifiers(Card...)`. So `.modifiers(...)` should be the canonical operation. But the `View` interface only has `with(ViewModifier...)`. 

So actually the deeper issue: the `View` interface should expose `modifiers(...)` (as either default method or the only way), and `with(ViewModifier...)` should be removed per the status claim. But that's a bigger change.

Actually wait — let me re-read the status claim: "the `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general modifier chain in favor of `.modifiers(...)`, and the `*Mod` shims ... are **removed**". So it claims `View.with(ViewModifier...)` was removed. But View.java:66 still has it! And `ViewBuilder` has `modifiers`. So maybe the intent was that `View` should have `modifiers(ViewModifier...)` (as a default) and NOT `with(ViewModifier...)`, but the removal wasn't fully completed, OR the intent is that `.modifiers(...)` only lives on ViewBuilder and plain Views use... hmm.

Let me think about what's the desirable, consistent design:
- The three operations are `with` (values), `modifiers` (modifiers), `children` (children).
- `ViewBuilder` exposes all three: `with(Consumer<C>)`, `modifiers(ViewModifier...)`, `children(View...)`.
- But the `View` interface (the open interface) — what should it expose? Currently it exposes `with(ViewModifier...)` (a default) for applying modifiers to a plain View value. That's inconsistent naming: `with` is "values", but here `with` is "modifiers".

Given the canonical DSL: `content.modifiers(A, B)` where `content` is any View (per DSL.md §5.6 Java column). So the `View` interface should have a `modifiers(ViewModifier...)` default method (returning `View`), and `with(ViewModifier...)` should be removed/renamed.

This is the cleanest fix per the spec. Then:
- `View.with(ViewModifier...)` → rename to `View.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` (default, returns `View`).
- But `ViewBuilder.modifiers(...)` returns `ViewBuilder<V, C>` — for `ViewBuilder` which already implements View, if View has a default `modifiers` returning `View`, then ViewBuilder's `modifiers` returning `ViewBuilder` would be a covariant override! That's fine in Java (covariant return types). So removing `with(ViewModifier)` and adding default `modifiers(ViewModifier)` on View interface works; ViewBuilder.modifiers already overrides it covariantly.

Wait, but ViewBuilder's `modifiers` isn't marked `@Override`. Currently View doesn't have `modifiers`, only `with`. If we add `default View modifiers(ViewModifier...)` to View, then ViewBuilder.modifiers(ViewModifier...) returning `ViewBuilder<V,C>` IS a valid covariant override (it would compile). Good.

Then all the demo/test sites that use `.with(Modifier...)` on a View/ViewBuilder should switch to `.modifiers(...)`.

Let me enumerate the fix sites:
1. `MusicPlayerView.java:110-112` — `PlayerBar.with(...).with(Border..., Shadow...)` → `.modifiers(Border..., Shadow...)`. Per chain order (modifiers first?), hmm — but the chain starts with `PlayerBar.with(p -> p...)`. Since these are values-first in the demo (the demo uses `X.with(...)` entry then children), what's the canonical? Looking at the issue #140 convention from prior work: "canonical order modifiers → with → children". So modifiers should come first. For PlayerBar:
```
PlayerBar
    .modifiers(
        Border.with(...),
        Shadow.with(10))
    .with(p -> p
        .trackIndex(...)...)
```
That aligns. But it's a bigger restructure. Alternatively just `.with(...)` → `.modifiers(...)` keeping order. Hmm. The user's complaint is specifically "Uses with for Modifiers" — i.e., modifiers are being applied via `with`. The minimal fix targeting the principle: use `.modifiers(...)` for modifiers.

But given issue #140 established "modifiers → with → children" as canonical chain order, and the current code does values `.with(p -> p...)` then modifiers `.with(Border...)` — both issues. Let me check what the OTHER demo views do for consistency: e.g., in MusicPlayerView line 110 the pattern `PlayerBar.with(p -> p...).with(Border, Shadow)` — the modifiers come after the with. In NowPlayingSidebar (line 58-62): `VStack.modifiers(Padding, Background, Frame).with(v -> ...)` — modifiers FIRST then with. So NowPlayingSidebar uses the canonical order (modifiers first), but MusicPlayerView's PlayerBar block uses `with(...)` then `with(Modifiers)` (wrong: uses with for modifiers AND order).

        .modifiers(

But careful: `with` is also used for values on static factories, and `ViewBuilder.with(Consumer<C>)`. The View interface's `with(ViewModifier...)` is only on the interface as an instance default. Renaming it to `modifiers` is consistent.

Per status.md claim that `View.with(ViewModifier...)` general modifier chain "are **removed**" — the intent was to remove it. The user asks: would `with -> children -> modifiers` be more SwiftUI-like?

Let me think about SwiftUI. In SwiftUI:
```swift
VStack(alignment: .center, spacing: 8) {
    Text("x").padding(16)
}
```
- Constructor params (values) come first: `VStack(alignment:spacing:)`
- Trailing closure = children: `{ ... }` comes right after constructor, enclosing children.
- Modifiers are chained on the *outside*: `VStack(...) { ... }.padding(16)` — the modifier wraps the whole container including its children.

So in SwiftUI, the natural order is: values → children → modifiers. The trailing closure (children) is part of the construction, and modifiers wrap the completed structure.

Example:
```swift
VStack(spacing: 8) {
    Text("Hello")
    Text("World")
}
.padding(16)
.background(.blue)
```

So yes — `with -> children -> modifiers` IS more SwiftUI-like, because in SwiftUI the modifier applies to the fully-constructed view (including its content), and children are part of construction, not decoration.

**Single-value shortcuts.** A view or modifier whose config designates a
**primary value member** MAY also expose `with(value)` / `with(Signal<T>)`
overloads that are pure sugar for the config-builder lambda:

```
Text.make("hi")            ≡  Text.make(t -> t.text("hi"))
Padding.with(16)           ≡  Padding.with(p -> p.uniform(16))
FontSize.with(sizeSignal)  ≡  FontSize.with(s -> s.size(sizeSignal))
```

A shortcut emits **byte-identical** opcodes and carries no extra semantics
(source-surface only — [§Conformance](#conformance)). The config-lambda form
(`with(c -> …)`) remains canonical and always sufficient.

- **Only a designated primary member** gets a shortcut. A config with **several
  equivalent members** (`Padding` edges, `Offset`/`Position` x+y, `Gauge`
  value/min/max, `Border` color+width(+radius), `FixedSize` horizontal+vertical,
  `AspectRatio` ratio+mode, a control's value+range) has **no** shortcut — use the
  lambda. `Padding` is the exception that proves it: its single-value primary is
  `uniform`, and per-edge padding is the lambda.
- **Both forms exist where the member has both**: a raw value and a
  `Signal<T>` (same rule as the config setters above). A two-way control value is
  never a shortcut — it stays a `WritableSignal` config member.
- The Java realization declares the overloads per type (Java statics are not
  inherited); they delegate to the existing `with(Consumer<Config>)` factory, so
  there is exactly one construction path. The former `.of(...)` factories are
  **removed** — a shortcut (or the lambda / `.children(...)` / empty `with()` for
  config-less views) replaces every one.

Eligible members (non-exhaustive; the companion tables list the surface):

| Kind | Shortcut |

### The three operations

Every concrete view exposes the same three operations. They form one fluent
**builder**: any of the three may be the first call, and they may be chained in
any order. A later call overrides an earlier value for the same property.

| **children** | Supply the content subtree (content-bearing views only) | trailing closure `{ … }` |

The **canonical builder spelling** (the recommended form; per-language spellings
are in [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)) is:

```
ViewName.with { values }              // values   — a config-builder lambda
      .modifiers(modifier, ...)       // modifiers — varargs
      .children(view, ...)            // children  — varargs, content-bearing views only
```

```

            removed += 1

1: # Pathland DSL Authoring Contract
2: 
3: **Wire protocol version:** 1
4: **Status:** Draft
5: **Last Updated:** October 9, 2026
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## Purpose
10: 
11: This document defines the **authoring surface** — the SwiftUI-shaped DSL an
12: application developer writes — for every Pathland implementation. Where
13: [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md), and
14: [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) describe the **wire surface** (component types,
15: property ids, events, opcodes), this file describes the **surface in source
16: code**: how views, controls, modifiers, and state are *named*, *ordered*, and
17: *composed* so that any language can expose a conformant, idiomatic DSL.
18: 
19: A DSL in a new language is **conformant** when it:
20: 
21: 1. exposes the full surface catalogued here (views, controls, modifiers,
22:    signals, state);
23: 2. maps every DSL element to the exact protocol component/property/event
24:    documented in the companion specs (no re-interpretation, no reallocation);
25: 3. produces **byte-identical opcode output** for the same source tree as the
26:    reference implementations (see the [Generation
27:    contract](#9-generation-contract-for-a-new-language)).
28: 
29: ### Relationship to the other specs
30: 
31: | File | Role |
32: |------|------|
33: | [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md) | Wire format: categories, commands, 16-byte opcode layout, ring/arena, value types |
34: | [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md) | Which **views/nodes** exist and their component ids |
35: | [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md) | Which **modifiers** (properties) exist and how they encode |
36: | [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) | Which **core events** (raw inputs) exist and how they encode |
37: | [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) | Golden byte vectors |
38: | [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md) | Design-token catalog, resolution, and color-scheme contract |
39: | **DSL.md** (this file) | How an application **author** composes those into source code |
40: 
41: > **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
42: > in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. The Java DSL
43: > (`com.pathland.view`) and the Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) are the two reference
44: > realizations; the "Java DSL" / "Rust DSL" columns below record the **agreed
45: > reference shapes**, not implementation status. This document defines the
46: > contract only.
47: 
48: ### Two guiding rules
49: 
50: 1. **Stay as close to SwiftUI as possible.** View names, modifier names, and
51:    signature shapes mirror SwiftUI. Adapt only where the host language forces
52:    it (Rust snake_case + macros; Java camelCase + builders; Python kwargs), and
53:    never in a way that reorders or renames the canonical parameters.
54: 2. **State variables are signals.** Pathland does **not** use SwiftUI's
55:    `@State`/`@Binding` property wrappers. The view syntax is SwiftUI; the
56:    reactivity model is Angular-style signals (writable signals, computeds,
57:    effects, two-way bindings). A generated DSL MUST expose the signal surface
58:    of [§3](#3-state-model-signals).
59: 
60: ---
61: 
62: ## 1. Design principles (DSL-flavored)
63: 
64: These recap the protocol's non-negotiables in author-facing terms. A conformant
65: DSL must be *shaped* by them:
66: 
67: - **Declarative structure, never positions.** The DSL expresses `WHAT` — a
68:   `VStack`, a `HStack`, a `Text` — and constraint properties (spacing, padding,
69:   alignment, size hints). It never computes bounds and never emits rects.
70: - **Exactly three authoring operations.** Every view exposes the same three
71:   operations — **configure values** (§5.0 `with`), **apply modifiers**
72:   (`modifiers`), and, for content-bearing views, **supply children**
73:   (`children`). The three are a single fluent builder: any of them may be the
74:   first call and they may be chained in **any order** (see
75:   [§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)); a later call overrides an earlier
76:   value for the same property.
77: - **`body()` is evaluated once at mount.** A composite view declares its
78:   subtree once; reactivity comes from **signals**, never from re-evaluating the
79:   body. This is what lets the emitter produce fine-grained
80:   `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE` deltas instead of rebuilding the tree.
81:   The one sanctioned exception is a **structural container**
82:   ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)): its content is
83:   re-evaluated on a signal change and the emitter reconciles the retained
84:   subtree into `TREE` deltas.
85: - **Modifiers are decoupled from views — and never hard-bound to a view
86:   type.** Any modifier applies to any view (`.padding` works on a `Text` and a
87:   `VStack` alike), and any developer can **author a custom modifier in
88:   application code** (a `ViewModifier`) that applies to any existing view —

### 5.6 Custom modifiers (developer-authored)

In SwiftUI any developer can define a modifier that applies to **any** existing
view — and Pathland is the same. This is a **first-class, MUST** property of
every conformant DSL: modifiers are never hard-bound to a view type.

- **Applicable to any view.** A modifier works on a library primitive
  (`Text`), a container (`VStack`), a control (`Button`), a custom view, or an
  already-modified view. The same modifier value applies everywhere.
- **One mechanism.** Core and application-authored modifiers are the **same

- each candidate child wrapped in `<div data-pathland-fitcand="{i}" hidden>` (or with a class), and a `<style>` block scoped with `@container fitslot-{id} (min-width: T_i)` rules that unhide the matching band(s).

The `<style>` block can be emitted per-document (safely under a container-name scoping) or per-slot inline `<style>` inside the slot (wrapping each child). Simpler: emit ONE `<style>` block in head with rules for all fit slots, generated from FIT_QUERY thresholds + node ids. Since the HTML renderer decodes the full tree (`decode`), it can collect all fit slots and emit one `<style>` block.

But deltas: when FIT_QUERY changes or candidates change, the DOM client re-applies. Container query `min-width: 640px` etc are static rules from thresholds — the client mirrors them.

This is quite involved. Let me check how much the user wants vs. how big. Given it's a plan, I should present clear options with a recommendation and let the user decide the wire semantics (the crucial fork):

**Fork A (all candidates always on the wire)** — clean pure-function renderer, correct first paint, no TREE swaps for band changes on web, hidden candidates stay live, more bytes, spec change "children: at most one" → "children: all candidates; renderer shows by fit".

I'll recommend Fork A. Also need to handle: does the app still need FIT_CHANGED at all if CSS auto-selects on web? Yes — for app-side state (fitIndex drives e.g. effects, and non-web renderers). Keep FIT_CHANGED flow as-is (report on transitions from the ResizeObserver). But the emitter should NOT swap children on FIT_CHANGED (children are all always present); it just sets fitIndex.

Actually wait, there's a subtlety about statelessness + "report only on transitions". Today the DOM client measures and reports FIT_CHANGED, app swaps. With all-candidates + container queries, the DOM client doesn't NEED to swap — the browser CSS handles visibility. But we still want FIT_CHANGED so the app's fitIndex stays correct. Keep ResizeObserver reporting transitions.

One more consideration: when band crossing happens purely via CSS, the visible candidate changes instantly. FIT_CHANGED then updates the app's fitIndex (no TREE swap).

Also, headless/non-web renderers: they already select locally via fit_index (GTK deferred). With all candidates on the wire, GTK would render ONE (it maps the selected child; but which? It needs the selection). Since GTK has no fit support yet (unmapped), unchanged concern.

Also, the CSS: does the shared STYLE need `container-type` support? It's inline per-slot. The `@container` rules must live in a `<style>` block. Also need `display: contents` wrappers? Candidate subtree is a full rendered subtree; wrap each candidate in its own `<div data-pathland-fitcand data-pathland-id?>`... but the DOM client keys nodes by data-pathland-id. Hmm, but the DOM client's hydrate/apply logic iterates `[data-pathland-fit]` and children; need it to know the candidate wrappers so CSS toggling survives deltas (e.g., a candidate's props update). Since candidates are real child nodes with ids, prop deltas apply fine (they're inside the wrapper). Removing a candidate removes the wrapper (client must delete wrapper too). I have enough understanding now. Let me think about the design carefully.

## The problem

Issue #141: over network, SizeThatFits may delay the first correct rendering. Today:
- Wire carries only the **selected** candidate (one child).
- SSR renders that single child (index 0 fallback by default).
- DOM client measures, derives fit, reports FIT_CHANGED; app swaps child → second frame.
- So first paint may show the wrong (fallback) variant until a round trip.

## The proposal (user's)

Render **all branches** of SizeThatFits in SSR, gate visibility with **CSS container queries** matching the Fit's minWidth thresholds. First paint is correct immediately (browser-side container query picks based on the slot's real width). After hydration, keep the delta flow working.

## Key architectural facts discovered

1. **Wire today carries one child** (spec: "children: at most one", "only that child ever transmits"). The engine/Rust DSL/Java DSL all emit exactly the selected candidate.
2. So to render ALL branches in SSR, **the opcode stream must carry all candidates** — this is a protocol/spec change. OR the SSR renderer needs them some other way.

This is the crux. Two sub-options:
- **A) Change the wire**: SIZE_THAT_FITS transmits ALL candidates as children (each child = a candidate). The renderer picks the visible one via container query. FIT_CHANGED still flows for app-side selection state? Actually if all candidates are on the wire, the app no longer strictly needs to swap children on FIT_CHANGED — the renderer already has all candidates. But the FIT_CHANGED is still useful for the app to know the current selection (the app owns retained state). Hmm, actually the spec's whole design is "the app transmits only the selected child; candidates live app-side" — the point being bandwidth: don't transmit unselected subtrees. Transmitting all candidates changes that contract.

- **B) Keep wire as-is (one child), SSR renders all candidates by having access to all of them somehow**. But the Rust HTML renderer is a pure function of the opcode stream — it can only render what's transmitted. The candidates live app-side in the Java/Rust DSL, not on the wire. For SSR, the server builds the HTML from the opcode stream. So SSR cannot know about un-transmitted candidates unless:
  - the emitter emits them all (wire change), or
  - there's a separate SSR-only side channel.

The user explicitly said: "So render all branches of the SizeThatFits and then use css to only render the matching one." and "The container queries should match the Fit's specified." and "And then after first render it should hydrate and work with delta changes afterwards."

So they're proposing to render all branches. This implies a wire change: SizeThatFits children = all candidates. Then the renderer maps each candidate to a container-query-gated wrapper. First paint correct.

But wait — there's tension with the "delta changes afterwards" step. If we simply send all candidates always, then FIT_CHANGED no longer needs to trigger a child swap (all children are always there). The renderer shows the matching one via CSS. FIT_CHANGED becomes purely informational to the app (which may matter for app logic), or possibly still needed to keep the app's `fitIndex` signal in sync so other derived UI reflects it. Actually the app-side retained `fitIndex` still drives app logic (e.g. a computed that depends on which variant is shown), so FIT_CHANGED is still useful. But no TREE swap is needed over the wire after hydration — the candidates are all present from the start.

Hmm, but that contradicts the architecture principle "only changes travel" (an unchanged fit emits zero opcodes). With all-candidates-always model: an unchanged fit → zero opcodes (candidates unchanged). A candidate's content changed → emits that candidate's deltas even if it's not the visible one. That's a real tradeoff: transmitting all candidates means a background candidate's changes ride the wire even while invisible. For the music demo that's fine (small). But it changes the protocol contract.

Alternative middle ground: 
- **A1) Always transmit all candidates.** Cleanest conceptual model; SSR renders all; container queries gate visibility; FIT_CHANGED still flows for app state; no child swap ever. But bandwidth: always all subtrees. Browsers handle display:none fine. Protocol change: children: N (all candidates), plus the renderer uses container queries to show one.
- **A2) Transmit all candidates ONLY in the initial/SSR snapshot, then collapse to one-child + swaps on FIT_CHANGED.** More complex: after first render + connect, the server sends a full snapshot (or the client requests resync) that has only the selected child, and the client replaces the container-query presentation with the single-child delta model. This is messy and would cause a visible flicker/jump when the SSR's all-candidates present becomes one child. Not great.

Actually, let me reconsider what "container queries" buys for the LIVE client vs SSR. Container queries are a CSS feature: `@container (min-width: 640px)` applied to a wrapper gated by the slot. This works for BOTH SSR first paint AND live resize — the browser re-evaluates container queries on resize automatically. So the DOM client could ALSO use container queries instead of ResizeObserver+measure. Then FIT_CHANGED reporting still needs the derived index to send to the app: but actually, if the visible candidate is chosen purely by CSS, the DOM doesn't need to pick anything — the app's `fitIndex` signal... hmm, the app wants to know which one is shown (for its own logic), and to be honest the renderer is supposed to be stateless (must not retain app state). Displaying via container query is fine (it's output selection, arguably layout). But the app still needs FIT_CHANGED to update its retained selection (which other logic may read). And the renderer still needs SOME notion of "which is currently active" to report transitions.

But container queries + ResizeObserver: ResizeObserver on the slot still gives width → fit index → FIT_CHANGED. Or, we could drop the measure and just report the fit when the visible candidate changes (via mutation observer on container query application? awkward). Simplest: keep the existing ResizeObserver + fitIndexFor to report FIT_CHANGED transitions, but let CSS container queries handle VISIBILITY. The reports keep the app's fitIndex in sync (no swap needed if all candidates, or swap is a no-op / never happens).

Wait — if all candidates ride the wire and the DOM shows via container query, do we even need FIT_CHANGED? The app-side retained `fitIndex` drives... in the current Java DSL FitSlot, fitIndex is a WritableSignal class-saved as `node.fitSelection`. Its structuralContent only renders the selected. If we move to "all candidates always present", FitSlot just always renders all candidates and fitIndex is only informational. The emitter's reconcileSlot/restoreFitSelection logic would change to not swap. But keeping FIT_CHANGED is still valuable: the app can bind to the current fit (e.g. a computed signal) and it's part of the retained semantic ("the slot knows its selection"). Also non-CSS renderers (GTK, future) need the selection conveyed to them... actually no—non-CSS renderers measure themselves and pick locally (per spec). FIT_CHANGED is app-<->renderer sync. Keep it.

OK so I think the design is:

**Design: SizeThatFits transmits all candidates as children; HTML renderer gates each in a container-query wrapper; FIT_CHANGED continues for app-side selection state (no TREE swap on the web anymore).**

Let me reconsider whether to keep the child-swap so that non-web renderers and network stay lean. The issue is literally about SSR over network. The simplest, most robust model:

### Option A (recommended): All candidates as children, container-query visibility on the web
- **Protocol/spec change**: `SIZE_THAT_FITS` children = all candidates (N children). `FIT_QUERY` thresholds still riding. The selected index is no longer conveyed by "which child"—the renderer picks via measure/container-query and reports FIT_CHANGED, and the app keeps `fitIndex`. An unchanged fit emits zero opcodes (candidates unchanged). 
  - Hmm, but "only one child on the wire" is a real bandwidth optimization AND the spec in PRIMITIVES.md/LAYOUT.md says children: at most one. Changing it touches: spec (DSL/PRIMITIVES/LAYOUT/OPCODE?), Java FitSlot render + emitter, Rust pathland-view SizeThatFits, TS client, HTML renderer, golden fixtures, conformance vectors.
  - The tradeoff: transmitting every candidate's subtree (background music demo candidates are large-ish: full controls row). But 2 candidates each. Fine.
- **HTML renderer**: slot div becomes a container (`container-type: inline-size`), each candidate wrapped in `<div style="@container ...>`—wait, container queries can't be inline; they need a `<style>` block. Options:
  1. Emit a per-document `<style>` block with `@container (min-width: T_i) { ... }` rules keyed by slot id + candidate index. Generated from FIT_QUERY (thresholds) and candidate count.
  2. Use inline `style` with `display:none !important` overridden by a `<style>` block — still needs a style block.
  - Actually the cleaner approach: each candidate wrapper gets `data-pathland-fit-cand="i"` and we generate container-query rules. Container query needs a `container-type` on the slot and the query uses `@container (min-width: Xpx)`. The bracket ranges: fit rule is `max{ i : thresholds[i] <= width }`. So candidate i is visible when `thresholds[i] <= width < thresholds[i+1]`. Container queries support both min and max: `@container (min-width: T_i) and (max-width: T_{i+1}-1)` but boundaries/float thresholds and "exactly equal picks lower index" matter. Actually since thresholds are floats in logical points, and widths are in css px (which are also logical points-ish at DPR... no, CSS px ARE logical/device-independent). Browser width matches thresholds in px. Boundaries: equal threshold → higher index wins (larger index = higher threshold; but if thresholds equal t==t, lower index wins). Container query ranges can express this but "less than next threshold" for floats: `max-width: T_{i+1}` is inclusive of the boundary, which would wrongly show candidate i at width == T_{i+1}. Need `max-width: T_{i+1} - 0.1px`? Hacky. 

  Hmm. This is where container query ranges get fiddly. But actually container queries support the newer comparison syntax? `@container (width < 640px)` — yes! Modern container queries support range syntax like media queries: `@container (width < 640px)`, `(640px <= width < 1024px)`. Browser support: Chrome 111+, Safari 17+, Firefox 121+ (2023-2024). Reasonable. So:
    - candidate i visible when `thresholds[i] <= width && width < thresholds[i+1]` (with the fit rule's tie-break only complicating equal-threshold duplicates). For the LAST candidate: `width >= thresholds[last]`.
    - equal thresholds: lower index wins → a duplicate band: candidate i with equal threshold as i+1 → only i ever shows (i+1 never). Range for i+1 would be empty. The fit_index rule already handles: for equal thresholds, selected stops at the lower. We can just emit rules that mirror fitIndexFor exactly, including skipping duplicates.
  - So generate per-slot CSS: `@container pl-{slot-id} (width >= T_i) and (width < T_{i+1}) { [data-pathland-id=...] }`. Simpler: candidate wrapper spans. Or apply to the child's own wrapper div with data attribute.

- **TS client**: 
  - Hydrate: candidate wrappers already have correct container queries from SSR's `<style>` block. But the client ALSO needs to emit the style rules when creating slot nodes at runtime (or maintain a `<style data-pathland-fit>` element it updates). Since deltas can create NEW SizeThatFits slots (rare but possible), the client should generate the same CSS. Or simpler: keep the ResizeObserver but instead of toggling display, just report FIT_CHANGED. Visibility handled by container query CSS consistently between SSR+runtime. So client needs to generate/update the style block.
  - Actually, simpler unified approach: the DOM client maintains a `<style data-pathland-fit>` element and writes `@container` rules, regenerated whenever FIT_QUERY changes. On hydrate it re-uses the SSR-generated rules (they're already in the doc). On new slots it adds rules.
  - FIT_CHANGED: still report transitions (via ResizeObserver) so app fitIndex stays in sync. No structural child swap needed anymore (all candidates present). This significantly simplifies the client (no delete/insert of slot children on fit change) AND kills the flash-of-wrong-variant.

- **Java FitSlot**: render all candidates as children. Keep FIT_QUERY. Keep fitInput (FIT_CHANGED sink) updating fitIndex; but structuralContent now returns... all candidates? Actually node.children = all candidates always; fitInput just updates the signal (app logic) — no structural reconcile swap. OR keep structuralContent returning the selected only for non-web renderers? That bifurcates. If the wire always carries all candidates, then GTK (whenever it implements fit) measures and shows one. But GTK fit is deferred. So web is the only fit consumer. Making the wire carry all candidates uniformly is cleanest and future-proof: every renderer receives all candidates and selects locally. That matches statelessness better (renderer picks from what it has).

Wait, but then "renderer must not retain app state" — the slot having all candidates and showing one via CSS: the *visible one* is layout output. Fine.

But there is a real downside: **bandwidth + the "only changes travel" principle**. Candidates that never show still transmit their full subtree on mount and on any internal change. The spec explicitly engineered to avoid this ("the others never transmit"). The user's request is literally to overrule this for first-presentation correctness. I should surface this tradeoff clearly and let the user decide (they already proposed it, so they've accepted it — but I should still note the delta-efficiency implication, e.g. background candidate changes ride the wire while hidden).

Actually re-reading the user: "render all branches of the SizeThatFits and then use css to only render the matching one. The container queries should match the Fit's specified. And then after first render it should hydrate and work with delta changes afterwards."

"work with delta changes afterwards" — I think this means: after the first (SSR) render, the normal delta/hydration flow continues to work (as today). It does NOT necessarily mean "keep the child-swap model". But it COULD mean: SSR renders all (so first paint is correct), but after hydration reconnect to the single-child delta model? That would cause a transition where SSR shows all-candidates and then a full snapshot collapses to one child... which reintroduces the flash. I think the coherent end-state is all-candidates-always (Option A1), and "delta changes afterwards" = normal SET_TEXT/PROPERTY/TREE deltas keep applying to whatever is on screen, FIT_CHANGED keeps the app signal in sync.

Hmm, but actually there's an even lighter-weight interpretation that avoids the wire change:

### Option B: SSR-only — all candidates rendered ONLY in SSR HTML, generated by giving the HTML renderer access to candidates via a separate mechanism
The Rust HTML renderer is a pure function of opcodes. It can't see un-transmitted candidates. The Java server (PathlandSession) authors the app tree — it KNEW all candidates at authoring time (the Java views). It could render the SSR HTML not through the opcode stream but... no, SSR HTML is built by `render_document(opcodes, strings, root)`. To include all candidates, the opcode stream must include them. No way around it without violating the pure-function renderer principle. So the wire change is essentially required by the user's approach. (Alternatively the server could emit a special "SSR probe" frame containing all candidates, but that's a bespoke side-channel — worse.)

So **Option A is the way**. Let me also decide:
- Keep FIT_CHANGED as a real event (transitions on ResizeObserver) — yes, app reads fitIndex. But there's a wrinkle: FIT_CHANGED is host→guest; the guest (app) keeps the canonical fitIndex; the renderer is stateless (doesn't store it — it stores measured width as layout, and "lastIndex" only as a send-coalescing cache, which is allowed as output cache). Fine, unchanged.

But wait: there's an important subtlety about statelessness + container queries. The renderer's *visible* candidate is determined by CSS, not by stored JS state. That's actually MORE stateless than today (today the DOM client computes index in JS from measured width; with container queries the browser computes it). Good for the principle. The DOM client still needs the ResizeObserver ONLY to emit FIT_CHANGED transitions (reporting), not to change visibility. 

Actually — could FIT_CHANGED also be driven by observing which candidate is visible? No, simpler to keep ResizeObserver.

Now, the container-query CSS generation. Where do rules live?
- SSR: the renderer can emit a `<style data-pathland-fit>` block (like the tokens block) containing `@container name (…) { … }` rules. Needs slot container-name uniqueness (id-based) since nested slots.
- The wrapper: candidate children need to be individually selectable. If SizeThatFits has N children, render each child wrapped in a div `data-pathland-fit-cand="i"`. But careful: adding a wrapper changes the layout transparency contract (slot forwards parent's align/justify). Wrapper should be `display: contents` by default, hidden (`display: none`) when not matching → but you can't put `display:none` inside a `display:contents` wrapper's query if the wrapper itself is the gated element. Make the *wrapper* the gated element: default `display:none`, and when its band matches → `display:contents` (so candidates lay out exactly as the slot's flex children, preserving existing alignment behavior). Actually `display:contents` makes the wrapper transparent; the candidate inner element then participates directly in the slot flex layout. That preserves the current "layout transparent" behavior perfectly!
  - So: wrapper `style="display:none"`, container rule `@container pl-{slot} (min-width:T_i) { [data-pathland-id={wrapper}] { display:contents } }`. But the wrapper needs an id for the client to apply deltas to the child inside it. Hmm — if wrapper is a non-node element (not in the tree), the client's runtime renderer doesn't know about wrappers. For deltas that create children of a slot at runtime, the client creates the child element — but where does the wrapper come from?
  - Option: make the wrapper carry the node id and the child be inside without its own id conflict... but child nodes have ids too. Today slot id = div.pathland-ftf, child id = the candidate node. If we add a wrapper per candidate, we need the wrapper and the real element. The DOM client's apply() manipulates elements by `[data-pathland-id]`. We could:
    - wrapper: `data-pathland-id="{childId}"` + class `pathland-ftf-cand` + `display:none` default; and the real child element WITHOUT a data-id (pure content) inside it? But the client looks up elements by id to apply props. If the wrapper has the id, props apply to the wrapper — wrong (they must apply to the innermost element). Unless the wrapper is `display:contents` (transparent) and props applied to it still style it — with display:contents, inherited properties still flow, but properties like width/flex on the wrapper affect layout as if... display:contents element's own box styles apply to the box it "expands" into? Actually with display:contents, the element's box is dropped and descendants render as if they were children of the parent; styles set on the contents element (like width, flex) do NOT apply (no box). So applying node styles to the wrapper is wrong.
    - Better: keep two elements — wrapper div (no id, `pathland-ftf-cand`) and the id-carrying real element inside; wrapper gated by container query; the id element is the actual node. The client needs to know, when it inserts/deletes a slot child, to wrap it. And the SSR needs to produce the same wrapper structure. And when a slot child is deleted (a candidate removed), the client must remove the wrapper.
  
  This is getting complex on the client side. Alternative that avoids client-side wrapper management substantially: 

  **Gate via the child itself using container query + a data attr + generated rules that set `display:none` on all but the match.** But container queries can't target "all children except the matching one" easily without per-child rules. With rules per child using an attribute, yeah we're back to wrappers *or* child-level rules.

  Simpler idea: **put the container query on the slot, and make each candidate a child; emit rules that hide everyone, then show the band.** Each candidate needs a selector. If candidates keep their own element (id = candidate id), the rule can target `[data-pathland-fit-cand="i"]` where we add that attr to the candidate's OWN element at SSR and at runtime-create. But runtime-created children are created generically by element.ts per component — we'd add the cand attr when inserting into a slot as child index. And the rule toggles `display`. But the candidate elements have legit display styles (flex etc.) set inline; a `@container` rule with equal specificity should still win for `display` if we use `!important` or make it a class on the element. Complexity again.

Honestly, the cleanest is wrapper-divs managed on both sides:
- SSR: slot children wrapped in `<div class="pathland-ftf-cand" data-pathland-fit-cand="i">…real child…</div>`, default `display:none`, plus `<style>` with `@container` rules to `display:contents` the matching wrapper. The real child keeps its id.
- Client: when inserting a child under a slot (SIZE_THAT_FITS), wrap it in the same gated div; on delete, remove wrapper. When applying props, apply to the real child (which has the id) — the client's existing `getElementById`/parent lookup still finds the real child (wrapper has no id). 

But hold on — the existing client find logic: `container.querySelector('[data-pathland-id=...]')` and parent traversal. Inserting a child into the slot: the slot's single child currently is attached directly. With wrappers we must target the wrapper as insertion point but apply to inner. The client's apply for `CMD_INSERT_CHILD` / `CMD_ADD_CHILD` picks a reference node by id among the container's existing children (to insert before). With wrapper-divs, the reference elements are still found by their id attributes (real children), and `insertBefore(ref, wrapper)` logic: we need `ref.parentElement` = wrapper. Because wrappers are display:contents, the real child's offsetParent/parentElement is the wrapper. `insertBefore` on the slot container with a wrapper `ref.parentElement` works. Doable but fiddly.

Given the scope, I think the plan should present the architecture and decompose into concrete steps, and explicitly call out the wrapper strategy and the CSS generation (style block, container-name, range syntax), plus the spec updates and test updates, and let the user confirm the key semantic changes:
1. Wire change: slot transmits all candidates (children = N). (Confirmed by user's proposal.)
2. FIT_CHANGED remains, no child swap on web (all candidates present); keep signal for app state.
3. Delta-efficiency tradeoff (background candidates' changes ride the wire) — acceptable for correctness.

Let me also double check whether there's an alternative: keep sending 1 child but have SSR render all by having the EMITTER, for the SSR document build, emit all candidates. But the emitter is the same for SSR and live; no separate code path. So no.

Also consider: what about renderers without container-query support (SSR conformance html-golden; and GTK is out of scope). The SSR HTML itself only needs CSS; the html-golden fixtures would change to include wrappers+style.

Also FIT_CHANGED cadence: "reports only on transitions" — the DOM client ResizeObserver cadence is unchanged.

Let me also think: does the app still need the child-swap AT ALL in the all-candidates model? The Java FitSlot's structuralContent renders all candidates; the emitter no longer swaps. But the Java `FitSlot` uses `fitSelection` to... only for its own render? If we always render all, `structuralContent` returns all candidates. `node.fitSelection` / `restoreFitSelection` logic becomes obsolete on the web but might still be useful to keep the signal correct. Actually since children are now all candidates always, restore-fit-selection no longer applies. The Rust DSL `fit_index` field also becomes vestigial (it selects which subset to emit — now emits all). We keep the fields but stop gating emission, OR keep gating for NON-web renderers? Statelessness says renderer decides; app just provides candidates + thresholds. Cleanest: emit all, always. The Java fitIndex signal still updates from FIT_CHANGED (app can read current fit for effects) — keep that.

But one more subtlety: the spec says before first measure the app renders index 0. With all candidates present, "index 0 shown" happens automatically via container query at width < first real threshold OR if no thresholds, all plus width>=... hmm: candidate 0 has minWidth 0; container query `width < T_1` shows 0; else 1. If thresholds are [0, 640]: 0 shows when `0 <= width < 640` → "compact" style. Equivalent. Good.

Now, is there a risk that container queries with `display:contents` inside a flex slot where the slot is `display:flex; flex-direction:inherit` etc. — the candidate becomes a flex item of the slot (as today) when its wrapper is contents. 

Also: `container-type: inline-size` on the slot. Today slot is `display:flex; ...; flex:1 1 auto`. Adding `container-type: inline-size` (and `container-name: pl-{id}`) makes it a size container. Its own width = filled width (good, that's the measuring unit). Container query reads its width. 

Edge: `container-type: size` requires explicit dimensions? `inline-size` only requires inline size be non-auto — slot has `flex:1 1 auto` so it fills. Good.

Also SSR style block: generated per document in render_document head (like token_style). And the DOM client, for runtime-created slots, must add the same rules — maintain a `<style data-pathland-fit>` element and append rules for each slot id + FIT_QUERY change. Regenerate on data-pathland-fit change (FIT_QUERY SET_PROPERTY).
